statement: In 16 healthy adults who had rarely or never used GHB, one laboratory dose of GHB compared with placebo in a randomized, double-blind crossover study was associated with much worse simulated driving at the first drive after the dose: every participant had more collisions than after placebo (median 6.5 against 1), with more off-road accidents and more weaving in speed and lane position, and everyone rated themselves less able to drive. At the two later drives the same day no simulator measure was worse than after placebo, but at the middle drive people still rated themselves less able to drive. Four men who vomited after GHB and could not complete the first drive were replaced and left out, so impairment may be underestimated; the study gave one dose to people without tolerance, with no alcohol, in a simulator, so it cannot show when it is safe to drive after GHB, and driving the morning after a night-time dose was not tested. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: In a lab driving test, people who took GHB once crashed far more often than when they took a dummy drink, on the first drive after taking it. Later the same day their test driving was no worse than with the dummy drink, but some still felt unable to drive. Only 16 people were tested, all new to GHB, with no alcohol, so the study cannot say when driving becomes safe.
population: Healthy adults aged 21 to 45 who had rarely or never used GHB, light drinkers, in a laboratory study in San Francisco (16 people, 8 women)
exposure: One oral laboratory dose of pharmaceutical GHB
comparator: Taste-matched placebo in the same people on another day
outcome: Simulated driving (collisions, off-road accidents, speed and lane-position variability) and self-rated ability to drive, at three drives after the dose
magnitude: First post-dose drive: collisions median 6.5 (range 2 to 19) against 1 (0 to 4), p < 0.001, r = -0.62, more in all 16; off-road accidents p = 0.018, r = -0.42; speed deviation 4.09 against 2.76, p = 0.002, r = -0.54; lane-position deviation 1.93 against 1.23, p = 0.004, r = -0.51; self-rated ability median 4 against 1 on a 1 to 5 scale, p < 0.001. Second drive: simulator measures not different; self-rating still worse, p = 0.001. Third drive: no difference in either.

evidence.locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, No. of collisions and No. of off road accidents rows
evidence.extracted: At the first drive after GHB, every one of the 16 participants had more collisions than after placebo: median 6.5 (range 2 to 19) against 1 (0 to 4), Z = -3.526, p < 0.001, r = -0.62; off-road accidents increased in 7 participants and in none after placebo (Z = -2.375, p = 0.018, r = -0.42); pedestrian hits did not differ.

evidence.locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, Mean speed, Mean speed deviation and Mean lane position deviation rows
evidence.extracted: At the first drive after GHB, speed deviation 4.09 against 2.76 (Z = -3.051, p = 0.002, r = -0.54; greater in 13 of 16) and lane-position deviation 1.93 against 1.23 (Z = -2.896, p = 0.004, r = -0.51; greater in 13 of 16); mean speed did not differ.

evidence.locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Figure 1 legend
evidence.extracted: All participants rated themselves less able to drive at the first drive after GHB than after placebo (median 4 against 1 on a 1 to 5 scale, p < 0.001); at the second drive the difference remained (p = 0.001), with nearly a third of ratings at 3 or higher; at the third drive it no longer differed.

evidence.locator: Results › Driving Questionnaire and Simulator results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2
evidence.extracted: At the second and third drives after GHB no simulator outcome was significantly worse than after placebo; at the third drive speed deviation was greater after placebo (p = 0.017). Within the GHB arm, collisions, off-road accidents and both deviation measures at the first drive were worse than at baseline and at both later drives.

evidence.locator: Methods › GHB and Placebo Dosing, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 7th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Four men developed nausea and vomiting after GHB and could not complete the first post-dose drive; they were replaced and only the 16 completers were analysed. The authors list one dose only, no regular GHB use (possible tolerance), simulator practice effects and no correction for multiple comparisons as limitations.

risk_of_bias.note: Four participants made ill by GHB were replaced and excluded; GHB's effects make unblinding likely (RoB 2 high on the card).

indirectness.note: Worded for one laboratory dose in people without tolerance, in a simulator, and says what was not tested.

imprecision.note: 16 participants; the later-drive comparisons cannot exclude smaller impairment.

grade.reasoning: A randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study starts high; risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give low. The first-drive impairment is large and seen in every participant; the later-drive findings show only that no difference was detected. Worded as an association because of the low certainty. Status single study.

statement: In a systematic review of studies up to August 2020 (van Amsterdam et al., 2022; AMSTAR 2 critically low), GHB impaired memory and psychomotor performance while it was acting in laboratory studies, roughly in step with dose, the review classes these as studies of acute effects and says it is not yet known whether such effects fully wear off; for lasting effects, it describes a cross-sectional Dutch sample of 81 people: those who used GHB heavily and had had repeated GHB-induced comas did worst on verbal memory and reported more anxiety, stress, depression and impulsivity than people who used GHB regularly without comas and people who used other drugs but never GHB, and brain imaging differed. Two of the review's authors wrote the reports on that sample; the comparison cannot show whether GHB or the comas caused the differences, which may have existed before use, and no one has followed people over time to see whether they reverse. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Lab studies show that GHB affects memory while it is working. Nobody has tested thinking in the days after taking GHB once. One Dutch study found that people who used GHB a lot and had passed out from it many times had worse memory than others, but it could not show that GHB caused this, and nobody has checked whether it gets better.
population: People who use GHB recreationally (heavy use with repeated GHB-induced comas; regular use without comas) and volunteers in laboratory studies, in studies gathered by a systematic review
exposure: Heavy GHB use with repeated GHB-induced comas (lasting effects); laboratory doses (acute effects)
comparator: Regular GHB use without comas, and people with mild polydrug use who never used GHB (lasting effects); placebo or other drugs (acute effects)
outcome: Memory, psychomotor performance, self-reported mood and impulsivity, and brain imaging
magnitude: No effect sizes reported by the review. Lasting-effects sample: 81 participants in three equal groups; the coma group performed worst on verbal memory. Acute studies: 14 laboratory studies of 8 to 49 participants each, impairment at moderate and higher doses, little or none at the lowest doses tested.

evidence.locator: Results › 3.3 Residual Cognitive Impairment Following GHB-Use and GHB-Induced Comas, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: One Dutch research programme recruited 81 participants in three equal groups (heavy GHB use with multiple GHB-induced comas; regular GHB use without comas; mild polydrug use, never GHB); the coma group performed worst on verbal memory, reported more anxiety, stress, depression and impulsivity, and showed differences in brain activity during memory and emotion tasks compared with the other two groups; the group with regular use without comas showed resting-state connectivity changes compared with the never-GHB group.

No follow-up study of residual impairment after stopping GHB had been done, so reversibility is unknown; the authors state the brain abnormalities may have been present before GHB use and may be a risk factor for it.

evidence.locator: Results, opening sentence; 3.2 Acute Effect of GHB on Cognition in Human Studies, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: In 14 laboratory studies (8 to 49 participants each), GHB impaired digit-symbol, memory and psychomotor performance at moderate and higher doses, with modest or no effects at the lowest doses tested; memory impairment was less than with triazolam, pentobarbital or alcohol at the doses compared. The review classes all 14 as studies of acute effects, gives no test timings, and states it remains to be established whether the amnestic effects are reversible.
All six cited reports on the lasting-effects sample list F. Raposo Pereira and W. van den Brink as authors; both are authors of this review.

risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional comparison without described adjustment, reported second-hand by a critically low review that did not appraise it.

indirectness.note: Second-hand; one Dutch sample of people with heavy use and comas.

grade.reasoning: The lasting-effects evidence is observational (start low) and is rated down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, so very low. The acute laboratory findings are context; the claim does not rate them separately. Status single study: one sample reported in six papers.
